body: Hello. For about ninety days you will get one short note a day about becoming someone who spends time outdoors, wherever you live, a little at a time.
Today, step outside for two minutes. Front step, balcony or pavement, it all counts. Just notice the air on your face.
Notice how many hours you spent indoors yesterday. No judgement, just a rough count to start from.
Look out of the nearest window for a full minute. What is the sky doing? Which way are the clouds moving?
Being an outdoor person does not require hills or hiking boots. A city street with a tree on it is a perfectly good start.
Find the nearest patch of green to your home: a park, a churchyard, a verge, a canal path. Look it up today, even if you do not go yet.
Take your next phone call outside if you can. Pacing the pavement beats pacing the kitchen.
Notice what the weather is actually like today, rather than what the forecast said. Step out and check with your own senses.
Leave your phone in your pocket for the first five minutes of any time outside today. Let your eyes do the looking.
Try drinking your morning tea or coffee by an open window or door. Begin the day with a little outside in it.
Spot one bird today. You do not need to know its name. Watch what it is doing for as long as it stays.
Notice the excuses that come up when you think about going out: too cold, too busy, too tired. Write them down so you can see them clearly.
Pick a regular moment to step out each day, such as after lunch or before the evening meal. A fixed time saves deciding.
Take the slightly longer route somewhere today, one that passes a tree, a garden or open sky.
Notice the light at a time of day you usually miss it. Early morning and late afternoon look very different from midday.
Two weeks in. When did you feel most at ease outdoors so far? What made that moment work?
Today, sit on a bench for ten minutes with nothing to do. If that feels odd, notice the oddness and stay anyway.
Touch something natural on purpose today: bark, a leaf, a stone wall warmed by the sun. Notice its texture.
Go out in light rain with a decent coat. Wet weather has its own sounds and smells that indoor days never offer.
Look up. Rooftops, treetops and the tops of buildings hold details most people walk straight past.
Find one plant growing somewhere unlikely, such as a crack in the pavement or a gutter. Small wildness is everywhere.
Eat one meal outside this week, even a sandwich on a wall. Notice how it tastes compared with eating at a desk.
Listen for a few minutes outdoors and count how many different sounds you can hear, near and far.
Keep a coat, a hat and a pair of comfortable shoes by the door, ready. Fewer obstacles mean more trips out.
Note the time the sun sets today. Knowing it helps you plan your outdoor moments around the daylight.
If you work from home, try one task outside today, such as reading a document or sketching out ideas on a bench.
Visit a park you have never been to, even one a short bus ride away. New places make old habits feel fresh.
Notice one thing that has changed outside since you began: a tree budding, leaves turning, a puddle gone.
Swap one screen break for a window or doorstep break today. Same few minutes, a very different view.
Walk somewhere you would usually drive or catch a bus to, if it is practical and safe. See the route at a slower pace.
A month of stepping out. How many days did you manage some time outside? Write the number down and be pleased with it.
Plan a slightly longer outing for this weekend: an hour in a park, a riverside, a common or a local nature reserve.
Bring nothing to do on that outing. No podcast, no list. See what your attention finds when it is left alone.
Choose a single tree near you and decide to visit it regularly. Over the coming weeks, watch how it changes.
When you feel restless indoors, try stepping out for five minutes before reaching for your phone. Notice which helps more.
Learn the name of one wild plant or bird you see often. Naming things makes them easier to notice next time.
Go outside after dark today, even briefly. Look for the moon, a star or the glow of streetlights on wet ground.
Invite someone to join you for a stroll or a coffee in the park. Shared time outdoors is often easier than a sit-down chat.
Notice the season in small signs: the angle of the sun, what is flowering, what people are wearing on the street.
If cold puts you off, dress one layer warmer than you think you need. Being comfortable makes staying out far easier.
Find a spot with a wide view, such as a hilltop, a bridge or a top-floor car park. Spend a few minutes just looking out.
Notice what your thoughts do during time outside. Do they slow down, wander, or tidy themselves up?
Collect one small natural thing today, such as a fallen leaf or a smooth pebble, and put it somewhere you will see it indoors.
Try doing nothing but watching water for a few minutes: a river, a fountain, a canal or rain running down a drain.
Six weeks in. What has quietly become easier about getting out of the door? What still gets in the way?
Choose a morning this week to step out before you look at any screen. See how the start of the day feels without it.
Go out in weather you would normally avoid, such as wind, drizzle or grey cold, properly dressed. Notice it is rarely as bad as it looked from inside.
Find a local green space that holds volunteer days, such as tree planting or litter picking. Consider signing up for one.
Grow something small: herbs on a windowsill, a pot of bulbs on a step. Tending it will draw you outside more often.
Notice the difference between being outdoors and simply passing through outdoors. Today, linger somewhere on purpose.
Try a short outdoor walk to think through a problem. Moving through open space often loosens a stuck idea.
If your week is packed, look for outdoor pockets: the walk to the shop, the wait at the bus stop, the school gate.
Take a different way home and pay attention to the gardens, trees and birds along it, as though you were a visitor.
Visit a place with water or woodland within reach by public transport. Plan the trip today, even if you go next week.
Notice which kinds of outdoor places you enjoy most: busy parks, quiet corners, open fields, the seaside. Lean towards those.
On a day you feel low on energy, step out for just three minutes. Sometimes that is enough to shift the afternoon.
Watch a sunrise or sunset this week, start to finish if you can. Few things are so reliably worth turning up for.
Keep a simple outdoor log for a week: where you went, how long, and one thing you saw. Patterns appear quickly.
Find out what grows or lives in your area at this time of year. Then go out and look for one of them.
Two months in. Write down how you would describe your relationship with the outdoors now, compared with day one.
Try a short outdoor routine that suits you, such as a loop round the block after dinner. Repeating one route deepens your noticing.
Lie on the grass and look at the sky for a few minutes, if you have somewhere comfortable. It feels like a holiday in miniature.
When friends suggest meeting indoors, offer an outdoor alternative now and then: a walk, a market, a picnic.
Notice how you talk about the weather. Try describing a grey day by what it offers, not only by what it lacks.
Pick one weekend afternoon this month to spend largely outside, with a flask and a loose plan.
If you have children, nieces, nephews or a dog in your life, let them set the pace outdoors for once. Follow their curiosity.
Check the forecast for the week and circle the brightest hour on the calmest day. Make that your hour outside.
Find a spot where you can hear no traffic at all, even briefly. Notice what fills the space instead.
Leave your headphones at home for one outing. Let the soundtrack be whatever the place offers.
When you are indoors for long stretches, open a window and let some outside air and sound in. Stay connected even then.
Notice what pulls you back indoors early. Is it cold hands, boredom, a sense of guilt about time? Adjust for the most common one.
Try sketching or photographing one ordinary outdoor scene carefully. Looking closely is a skill that grows with practice.
Notice smells outdoors today: cut grass, wet pavement, bakery air, woodsmoke. Scent is a quick way to arrive somewhere.
Revisit your chosen tree. What is different since you first picked it? Note the changes in a line or two.
Go out on a day off without a destination. Turn left or right on a whim and see where you end up.
Ten weeks in. Is time outside now something you do, or something you are? Write one sentence about which it feels like.
Plan how your outdoor habit will survive the next change of season. What will you wear, and when will the light be best?
When a busy week threatens to keep you in, protect at least one short outing as you would any other appointment.
Share a favourite outdoor spot with someone who might enjoy it. Showing a place to others deepens your own fondness for it.
Notice how your sense of your neighbourhood has grown. Which corners do you know now that you barely knew before?
Spend a little time outside in the evening this week, listening to how the sounds change as daylight fades.
Think of the outdoor moments that have mattered most these weeks. What do they have in common?
Try a small outdoor first: a dawn walk, a swim in a lido, a picnic in the cold, a night under a clear sky. Something new to remember.
Notice if you now reach for your coat when you feel stuck, bored or tense. That reflex is the new habit settling in.
Write down your few simple rules for getting outside: how often, how long, and what to do on days you really do not feel like it.
When someone asks what you did at the weekend, notice whether being outside features in your answer more than it used to.
Choose one outdoor place to keep returning to over the coming year. Familiar ground rewards the people who keep visiting.
Picture a year from now. Where would you like your favourite outdoor hour of the week to be spent?
Look back at the list of excuses you wrote at the start. Which ones have lost their grip on you since then?
Nearly at the end. Step outside today and simply stand still for a minute, taking in a place you now know far better.
Notice that the outdoors has been there all along. What has changed is that you now make room for it.
That brings these ninety days to a close. Keep stepping out, in whatever weather and whatever place you find yourself, and let the outside stay part of who you are.
